overview: Weir Group is a Scottish (Glasgow-headquartered) engineering company and a global leader in mining technology, supplying highly engineered equipment and aftermarket parts/services used to extract and process minerals. Following the 2021 divestment of its Oil & Gas Division, Weir operates two continuing-operations segments - Minerals (pumps, crushers, mill liners, tailings/separation equipment) and ESCO (ground engaging tools for excavation, plus a growing Software Solutions business following the 2025 Micromine and Fast2Mine acquisitions) - with facilities in over 50 countries and roughly 12,000 employees serving essentially every major mine in the world.

business_model.summary: Weir sells highly engineered original equipment (OE) into mining and infrastructure customers, then captures a large, recurring, high-margin aftermarket (AM) revenue stream as that equipment wears out in abrasive processing environments (c.80% of group revenue is aftermarket, with >90% aftermarket capture rate on installed original equipment). The 2025 acquisition of Micromine (mining planning/decision software) and Fast2Mine adds a subscription-based Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR) layer, which was c.24% of Micromine's 2025 revenue. Growth is driven by installed-base compounding (aftermarket grows even when large OE project orders are lumpy), supplemented by bolt-on M&A.

revenue_streams.name: Minerals Division (pumps, crushers, mill liners, tailings)
ESCO Division (ground engaging tools, attachments, software)

business_model.customer_type: B2B - large global and regional mining companies (copper, gold, iron ore, battery metals producers) plus infrastructure/aggregates customers; concentrated among Tier 1 miners but no single-customer dependency disclosed
business_model.geographic_mix: North America 32%, South America 21%, Australia 15%, Africa & Middle East 14%, Asia Pacific (ex-Australia) 11%, Europe & Central Asia 7% of FY2025 sales

main_competitors: Chinese/regional low-cost pump and GET replicators
competitive_position.market_position: Global leader in slurry pumps (WARMAN brand) and a top-tier provider of comminution (crushers, HPGR) and ground engaging tools (ESCO); Metso is the closest direct competitor with a near-identical product overlap in crushing, screening and pumping, making mill-circuit trials the key competitive battleground

moat_factors.description: Once Weir's engineered equipment (e.g. WARMAN pumps, ESCO GET) is installed in a mine's circuit, customers default back to OEM spares for fit, reliability and total-cost-of-ownership reasons; Weir captures >90% of aftermarket spend from its own original equipment
Facilities within 200km of every major mine globally enable rapid parts delivery and support, which is difficult for new entrants or distant competitors to replicate
WARMAN, GEHO, ENDURON and ESCO brands are trusted, mission-critical specifications; Minerals wins over 90% of large mill circuit pump trials it competes in

Micromine and Fast2Mine acquisitions build an equipment-agnostic software layer (mine planning, monitoring) that could deepen customer lock-in and cross-sell, though this is still early-stage and unproven at scale
Global foundry/manufacturing network allows production shifting to lower-cost regions and navigation of tariffs, though this flexibility has created short-term cost/mix drag (seen in H1 2026 margins)

weaknesses: Exposure to a small number of commodities (copper, gold, iron ore together are the majority of revenue) ties fortunes to mining capex/commodity cycles
Low-cost and Chinese 'third-party replicator' competition in spare parts threatens aftermarket pricing over time
Original equipment orders are lumpy/project-based, creating quarter-to-quarter revenue volatility
Integration risk across a rapid run of 2025 acquisitions (Micromine, Townley, Fast2Mine, ESEL) occurring simultaneously
Net debt/EBITDA rose sharply (0.7x to 1.9x at FY2025, then 2.2x at H1 2026) following the debt-funded Micromine deal, above the normal 0.5-1.5x target range

growth_drivers: Structural, multi-decade demand growth for critical minerals (copper, lithium, nickel, cobalt, rare earths) driven by electrification, grid build-out, renewable energy and AI/data-centre power demand
Compounding aftermarket growth as the installed base of original equipment expands, independent of large project timing
Brownfield expansion and debottlenecking spend by miners maximizing output from existing operations amid high commodity prices
Digital/software expansion via Micromine (mining planning software, ARR growing >25% in 2026) and Fast2Mine, building a broader equipment-agnostic software platform across the mining value chain
Bolt-on M&A strategy (Townley - North American phosphate/foundry capacity; ESEL - full ownership of Chile JV/direct-to-customer in world's largest copper market) expanding geographic reach and margin

Performance Excellence self-help program - cumulative savings target raised to £90m (from original ~£113m total program cost, down from £120m), supporting margin expansion toward >20% operating margin sustainably from 2026

New product launches (ENDURON Optimil Vertical Stirred Mills, WARMAN MCR2 pump, Nexsys GET system, Production Master buckets) designed to lower energy/water use and total cost of ownership for customers

business.description: Weir's principal risk register identifies market risk from commodity price/macro volatility (copper, gold, iron ore, nickel, lithium, oil sands) directly affecting customer capex and OE order flow
Group identifies rising presence of low-cost competitors with improving quality, plus third-party parts replicators, as a principal risk to pricing and margins
Failure to keep pace with digital, AI-enabled or disruptive processing technologies could erode Weir's market-leading positions over time

Jon Stanton (CEO since 2016, credited with the Oil & Gas divestment and pivot to mining hardware/software) steps down 1 August 2026, succeeded by internal Minerals Division president Andrew Neilson - an execution risk during a period of heavy acquisition integration

financial.description: Net debt/EBITDA rose to 1.9x at FY2025 and 2.2x at H1 2026 (above the 0.5-1.5x target range) following the AUD 1.3bn debt-funded Micromine acquisition plus Townley, Fast2Mine and ESEL; management guides a return toward 1.5x by end of 2026

Free operating cash conversion fell to 41% in H1 2026 (from 62% in H1 2025) on inventory build for production transfers and customer payment delays, though full-year guidance of 90-100% was reiterated
Reported sterling revenue and profit are subject to material currency translation headwinds (£22m PBT headwind in FY2025) given the global, largely USD/AUD/local-currency-denominated business
A US subsidiary facing asbestos-related claims entered Chapter 11 in 2025 and was deconsolidated; residual provisioning/reputational tail risk remains, inherited from the pre-2021 portfolio
UK and North American defined benefit schemes, though the UK Main Plan is currently in surplus with no required deficit contributions

regulatory.description: US tariff regimes required active supply-chain and pricing management in 2025-26; political risk register flags tariff/regulatory volatility as a top concern
Operating in >50 countries including some politically sensitive jurisdictions creates sanctions and country-risk exposure, managed via a no-tolerance policy on sanctions breaches
Evolving UK Corporate Governance Code (Provision 29, effective 2026) and ISSB-aligned climate disclosure requirements add compliance cost, though Weir already holds a CDP Climate 'A' rating

Explicit principal risk given reliance on global IT systems, increasing AI-enabled threat actors, and regulatory requirements evolving around data/AI governance, compounded by acquisition integration risk (inherited vulnerabilities)

macro.risk: Mining capex cycle / global growth slowdown
macro.description: A broad economic slowdown or fall in critical mineral demand would reduce both OE project awards and, with a lag, aftermarket intensity, even though aftermarket is relatively inelastic to commodity prices

Copper (~23-30% of exposure), gold (~11%), iron ore (~10%) price swings directly affect miner production economics and capex appetite; nickel/lithium/oil sands exposure has already seen subdued demand in 2025-26
Middle East conflict disrupted ESCO dredge-point demand and tungsten supply chains in 2025-26; broader geopolitical fragmentation affects supply chains, tariffs and localized mine-site disruptions

Moderate direct sensitivity via higher financing costs on increased post-acquisition debt (net interest expense guided at ~£90m for FY2026, declining to ~£70m by 2028); indirect sensitivity via financing costs for miners' capex plans

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Structurally positive: IEA and industry forecasts point to rising multi-decade demand for copper, lithium, nickel, cobalt and rare earths driven by electrification, grid build-out, renewables and AI data-centre power demand, with declining ore grades and long mine lead times creating persistent supply constraints that favor productivity-enhancing technology providers like Weir
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high at the OE/project level (tied to mining capex cycles and commodity prices) but materially dampened at the group level by the c.80% aftermarket mix, which is driven by non-discretionary spare parts spend largely inelastic to commodity prices
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low-to-moderate - mainly via financing costs on debt following the 2025 acquisition spree, and indirectly via the cost of capital for mining customers' expansion projects
key_input_costs: Tungsten (price spikes/export restrictions from China in 2025-26)

recent_developments.event: H1 2026 results: orders +8% (constant currency), revenue +5%, but adjusted operating margin fell 100bps to 18.8% on product mix/production-transfer timing; free operating cash conversion dropped to 41%; net debt/EBITDA at 2.2x; FY2026 guidance (constant currency revenue, profit and margin growth; 90-100% cash conversion) reiterated

CEO succession announced - Jon Stanton (CEO since 2016) to step down 1 August 2026 after a decade leading the pivot away from Oil & Gas into mining hardware/software; succeeded by Andrew Neilson, current president of the Minerals Division, who joined Weir in 2010 and previously led ESCO's integration

Q1 2026 trading update: Group orders +4% (constant currency); ESCO OE orders +49% on exceptional bucket demand; completed acquisition of remaining 50% of ESEL (Chile foundry JV); FY2026 guidance reiterated despite rising Middle East geopolitical tension

FY2025 annual results: orders +7% to £2,598m, revenue +6% to £2,565m, adjusted operating margin +150bps to 20.2%, statutory profit after tax -21% to £248m (prior year benefited from a one-off US tax credit); ROCE fell 140bps to 17.9% following heavy 2025 acquisition spend; final dividend of 22.1p (full year 41.7p, +4%)
Agreed to buy out ESCO's Chilean JV partner (ESEL foundry), completing in Q1 2026, positioning Weir for a direct-to-customer strategy in the world's largest copper-producing country
Completed acquisition of Fast2Mine (Brazil) for BRL 172m (~£25m), expanding the Software Solutions/digital portfolio
Completed acquisition of Townley Engineering & Manufacturing (US foundry/phosphate exposure) for US$150m (~£111m), expanding North American foundry capacity and phosphate market access

A US-based subsidiary carrying legacy asbestos liabilities was placed into Chapter 11 bankruptcy and deconsolidated, resulting in a £19.8m exceptional gain and removal of the associated provision from the balance sheet

Completed the transformational acquisition of Micromine (mining planning/decision software) for an enterprise value of AUD $1.3bn (~£624m), funded via a new AUD term loan facility, materially increasing leverage and establishing Weir's entry into mining software at scale

guidance.as_of: H1 2026 Interim Results (29 July 2026) and Q1 2026 Trading Update (30 April 2026)

items.target: Mid-single-digit organic constant currency growth, plus acquisition contributions
items.notes: Reiterated at H1 2026 despite H1 revenue growth of only +5% constant currency; management expects H2 weighting consistent with 2025 pattern

H1 2026 margin was 18.8% (down 100bps YoY) on product mix and delayed production-transfer savings; management expects margin recovery in H2 as mix improves and remaining Performance Excellence savings land
Raised from the original £90m target structure with total program cost reduced to £113m (from prior estimate of £120m); £66m achieved by Q1 2026, £72m by H1 2026 (incremental £13m in H1)
H1 2026 conversion was only 41% due to working capital build for production transfers and customer payment delays; management expects reversal in H2

items.target: Return toward normal operating range of 0.5x-1.5x (expected ~1.5x by year end 2026)
items.notes: Stood at 1.9x at FY2025 and 2.2x at H1 2026 due to acquisition funding (Micromine, ESEL) and cashflow phasing
Reflects higher post-acquisition debt load, expected to normalize as leverage reduces
Longstanding investment case target reiterated across FY2025 annual report and FY2026 interim guidance

items.target: Payout of c.33% of adjusted EPS
items.notes: FY2025 full-year dividend 41.7p (+4%); H1 2026 interim dividend 20.0p (+2%)

guidance.management_commentary: Outgoing CEO Jon Stanton said H1 2026 performance was 'in line with our expectations' with Q2 acceleration from market share gains, new product wins (Vertical Stirred Mills, WARMAN MCR2 pump) and recent acquisitions, and that the full-year outlook is 'underpinned' by a large orderbook (book-to-bill 1.12) and strong H2 pipeline visibility. He expressed confidence that incoming CEO Andrew Neilson, previously head of the Minerals Division, will continue the growth strategy. Management flagged that H1 margin and cash-conversion weakness was driven by temporary production-transfer and mix effects expected to reverse in H2, and that supply-chain disruption (Middle East conflict, Chinese tungsten export restrictions) has been managed without major impact to customers.

bull_case: Resilient, aftermarket-dominated (c.80% of revenue) business model provides predictable, high-margin, recurring cash flow that is largely inelastic to short-term commodity price swings, cushioning the cycle better than pure OE suppliers

Structural multi-decade tailwind from critical minerals demand (copper, lithium, nickel) driven by electrification, grid buildout and AI/data-centre power needs, with long mine lead times and declining ore grades favoring incumbent technology/service providers

Successful, well-executed M&A strategy (Micromine, Fast2Mine, Townley, ESEL) is building a genuine software/digital layer (ARR growing >25%) on top of the hardware franchise, diversifying revenue and deepening customer lock-in at attractive returns (post-tax returns expected to exceed cost of capital within three years per Weir's own M&A hurdle)
Performance Excellence program continues to compound margin gains (target: operating margin sustainably above 20% from 2026) even as the group scales through acquisitions

Consensus analyst sentiment is strongly positive (predominantly Buy ratings from Citigroup, Jefferies, Berenberg, JPMorgan, Panmure Gordon) with price targets implying meaningful upside from recent trading levels
bear_case: Leverage has risen sharply post-Micromine (net debt/EBITDA 1.9x at FY2025, 2.2x at H1 2026, above the 0.5-1.5x target range), leaving less balance-sheet flexibility and refinancing/interest-rate risk if commodity markets turn down before deleveraging completes

H1 2026 showed margin compression (18.8%, -100bps) and a sharp fall in free operating cash conversion (41% vs 62% prior year) from production-transfer disruption and working-capital build, raising execution risk around the heavy, simultaneous integration of four 2025-26 acquisitions

CEO transition (Jon Stanton departing after a decade, succeeded by internal candidate Andrew Neilson from 1 August 2026) introduces leadership continuity risk at a critical point in the digital/M&A strategy

Ultimate dependence on mining capex cycles and a narrow set of commodities (copper, gold, iron ore); a sustained commodity price downturn or global growth slowdown would still pressure original equipment orders and, with a lag, aftermarket intensity

Competitive intensity from Metso's near-identical product overlap plus low-cost/Chinese replicators threatens pricing power in both OE and aftermarket parts over time, and the stock's valuation already prices in continued above-market growth and margin expansion
